newsitem.title: INDIA: India's policymakers quiver over boiling oil pool.
newsitem.headline: India's policymakers quiver over boiling oil pool.

text.p: Taking a hard decision like raising oil prices does not come easy in the world's largest democracy, and India's policy-makers will take a third crack at the red hot issue on Tuesday.
Few oil sector analysts nurtured hopes that the United Front government's steering committee would find a way to whittle down the $4.9-billion debt to oil companies this week.
"The oil sector is so politically sensitive we cannot apply the general rule that economic reforms have become depoliticised in India," Tridib Pathak, at UBS Securities Pvt Ltd, told Reuters.
No party inside or outside Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-member coalition wants to burn potential votes by favouring a price rise when an election could come at any time.

The steering committee failed at its last two sessions to decided what to do about the oil pool account deficit, the money owed to oil companies for selling petroleum products below market prices to support India's subsidy regime.
And the meeting planned for Tuesday has been deferred twice already and could be again, officials said.

Shrivatsa Kumar, analyst at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking had no hopes of a breakthrough this week, but said action was needed urgently as oil companies faced a payments crunch for crude needed to keep refineries running.
"The government must take a bold step, and the sooner the better," Kumar said.
Some analysts expect the steering committee to recommend a petroleum product price rise of less than 10 percent and a mix of other measures, including lower import tariffs for crude and products.
Kumar believed an average price rise of 12-15 percent was needed, but others were tired of the guessing game.
"I've stopped taking bets on oil prices," said Subra Subramaniam, chief analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Bombay, adding that politics would play the deciding role.
Gujral's government is safe for now, propped up by Congress. But a split in his own Janata Dal party at the weekend showed that India does not possess political stability.
The breakaway faction of the Janata Dal has pledged support for Gujral, but it is one more fissure in the centre-left coalition.
The main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Congress, the second largest party, have both come out against price rises.
And inside the coalition, the leftist parties have remained staunchly opposed to any increase that would hit India's poor.
Subramaniam said any decision on oil prices may depend on whether Gujral gives ground to his allies on the left, given the split in his own party.
The finance and petroleum ministries have both previously put forward strategies that make price rises unavoidable.
But analysts said Tuesday's meeting had to present a more long-term plan for tackling the oil pool deficit to make it more palatable to their partners, analysts said.
For that reason most analysts have pared back expectations from the 15-25 percent price rises mooted in the past few months.
"There will be a single digit price hike in petrol, diesel and kerosene, and other industrial inputs like naptha and fuel oil," said P. Dhileepan, an oil analyst at NatWest Markets in Bombay.
"I don't think consumers will mind very much," he said.
Dhileepan estimated the deficit was currently around 175 billion rupees, up from 155 billion on March 31, the end of 1996/97 fiscal year.

UBS's Pathak said there could be a five to eight percent hike, but this was inadequate if the government was to make progress deregulating the oil sector and privatising the companies. He added that he expected no decision on Tuesday.
